pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 1: Computer Networks

How can a Samsung phone in Tamale send a message to an Apple laptop in London? Because every device follows the same set of communication rules arranged in layers. In this unit you will study the OSI model, the Internet and the World Wide Web, IP addresses and the Domain Name System.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.3.1.1** Identify the concept of computer networking for global communication.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.3.1.1.1** Describe the data communication models for networks.
- **B8.3.1.1.2** Describe the Internet, World Wide Web (WWW) and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 8.1 The OSI Model
- 8.2 The Internet, the WWW, IP Addresses and DNS

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC9.1, CC7.5).

lessons.title: The OSI Model

pages.title: The OSI Model
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.3.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model;
- identify its seven layers;
- discuss how the layers ensure interoperability of different hardware.
A **protocol** is a set of rules that devices follow when communicating. A **data communication model** organises these rules into **layers**, each with a specific job. The best-known model is the **Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model**, published by the **International Organization for Standardization (ISO)** in 1984.
[[fig:c8-f12|Figure 11: The seven layers of the OSI model]]
| **No.** | **Layer** | **Function** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Application | Provides network services directly to the user’s applications | HTTP/HTTPS (web), SMTP/IMAP (email), FTP, DNS |
| 6 | Presentation | Translates data formats, encrypts/decrypts and compresses data so both sides understand it | JPEG, MP3, ASCII/Unicode, TLS encryption |
| 5 | Session | Opens, manages and closes communication sessions between applications | Logging in to a video call session |
| 4 | Transport | Breaks data into **segments**, numbers them, checks for errors and resends lost data | TCP (reliable), UDP (fast, e.g. live video) |
| 3 | Network | Gives logical addresses (**IP addresses**) and chooses routes between networks; data units are **packets** | IP, routers |
| 2 | Data Link | Moves **frames** between devices on the same network using physical (**MAC**) addresses; detects errors | Ethernet, Wi-Fi, switches, NICs |
| 1 | Physical | Transmits raw **bits** as electrical signals, light or radio waves | Cables, connectors, hubs, radio signals |

pages.title: The OSI Model (continued)
pages.body:
> 🎯 **BECE focus — Memory aids** From Layer 7 down to 1: **A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing. From Layer 1 up to 7: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.
## Why layers matter: interoperability
- **Interoperability:** devices from different manufacturers (Samsung, Apple, HP, Huawei) and different operating systems can communicate because each follows the same layer standards.
- **Modularity:** each layer can be improved or replaced without changing the others (e.g. moving from cables to Wi-Fi only changes Layers 1–2).
- **Easier troubleshooting:** technicians check layer by layer (“Is the cable connected? Does the device have an IP address?”).
- **Standardisation** encourages competition and cheaper equipment.
- Helps learners and engineers **understand** complex communication step by step.
When data is sent, each layer adds its own control information (a **header**), a process called **encapsulation**; the receiving device removes the headers layer by layer in reverse. The Internet itself uses the simpler **TCP/IP model** (4 layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access), which maps onto the OSI layers.
> 🧪 **Activity — Layer role-play**
Seven learners each represent one OSI layer. A “message” written on paper is passed down from Layer 7 to Layer 1, with each learner adding an envelope (header), then passed to another group of seven who remove the envelopes in reverse order. Discuss what each layer added.

pages.title: The Internet, the WWW, IP Addresses and DNS
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.3.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe the Internet and classes of IP addresses;
- explain the Domain Name System;
- distinguish IPv4 from IPv6, and the Internet from the World Wide Web.
The **Internet** is a global network of millions of interconnected computer networks that communicate using the **TCP/IP** protocols. It began as **ARPANET** in the United States in **1969**. The Internet carries many services: the web, email, messaging, video calls, online gaming, file transfer and streaming.
## Internet vs World Wide Web
| **Internet** | **World Wide Web (WWW)** |
|---|---|
| The global **network infrastructure**: cables, routers, servers and protocols | A **service** that runs on the Internet: a collection of linked web pages |
| Started in 1969 (ARPANET) | Invented by **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN in **1989**; public in 1991 |
| Supports email, VoIP, file transfer, the web, etc. | Uses **HTTP/HTTPS**, **HTML** and **URLs**, viewed with a web browser |
| Analogy: the road network | Analogy: the vehicles (one type of traffic) using the roads |
## IP addresses
Every device on the Internet needs a unique **Internet Protocol (IP) address**, just as every house needs an address for letters to be delivered.
[[fig:c8-f13|Figure 12: The structure of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses]]

pages.title: The Internet, the WWW, IP Addresses and DNS (continued)
pages.body:
**Classes of IPv4 addresses**
IPv4 addresses were originally divided into five **classes** according to the value of the first number (octet):
| **Class** | **First octet range** | **Default subnet mask** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 – 126 | 255.0.0.0 | Very large networks (few networks, millions of hosts each) |
| B | 128 – 191 | 255.255.0.0 | Medium to large networks (e.g. universities) |
| C | 192 – 223 | 255.255.255.0 | Small networks (up to 254 hosts), e.g. home and school LANs |
| D | 224 – 239 | — | Multicasting (sending to a group) |
| E | 240 – 255 | — | Experimental / reserved |
127.x.x.x is reserved for **loopback** testing (127.0.0.1 means “this computer”). **Private** address ranges used inside homes and schools are 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255. Today the Internet uses **classless addressing (CIDR)**, but the classes remain useful for learning.
**IPv4 vs IPv6**
|  | **IPv4** | **IPv6** |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 32 bits | 128 bits |
| Format | Four decimal numbers separated by dots, e.g. 192.168.1.25 | Eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, e.g. 2001:db8::8a2e:370:7334 |
| Number of addresses | About 4.3 billion: **running out** | About 3.4 × 10³⁸: practically unlimited |
| Features | Needs NAT to share addresses | Built-in security options (IPsec), simpler routing, auto-configuration |

pages.title: The Internet, the WWW, IP Addresses and DNS (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Finding your computer’s IP address**
1. Press **Windows + R**, type cmd and press **Enter**.
2. Type ipconfig and press **Enter**.
3. Look for **IPv4 Address** (e.g. 192.168.1.25) and **IPv6 Address** under your network adapter.
4. Alternatively: **Settings › Network & internet › Wi-Fi/Ethernet › Hardware properties**.
## The Domain Name System (DNS)
People remember names like www.ghana.gov.gh more easily than numbers. The **Domain Name System (DNS)** works like a **phonebook** for the Internet: just as a phonebook converts a person’s name into a phone number, DNS servers translate **domain names** into **IP addresses**.
[[fig:c8-f14|Figure 13: How DNS finds a website]]
| **Part of a URL: https://www.moe.gov.gh/news** | **Meaning** |
|---|---|
| https:// | Protocol (secure HTTP) |
| www | Sub-domain (World Wide Web server) |
| moe | Organisation’s domain name |
| .gov | Second-level domain (government) |
| .gh | Country code top-level domain (Ghana) |
| /news | Path to a specific page |
